title: Computer Awareness
description: 300 MCQs covering Basics of Computer, Networking and Internet, and Office Productivity Tools (MS Word, Excel, PowerPoint) for PSSSB Junior Engineer exam preparation.

questions.text: What is the smallest unit of data in a computer?
questions.expl: A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of data a computer can store, representing either 0 or 1.

questions.text: 8 bits are equal to one:
questions.expl: 8 bits together form 1 byte, the basic unit used to represent a single character.

questions.text: 1024 bytes are equal to one:
questions.expl: 1 Kilobyte (KB) = 1024 bytes, following the binary (base-2) counting convention used in computing.

questions.text: 1024 Kilobytes are equal to one:
questions.expl: 1 Megabyte (MB) = 1024 Kilobytes.

questions.text: 1024 Megabytes are equal to one:
questions.expl: 1 Gigabyte (GB) = 1024 Megabytes.

questions.text: 1024 Gigabytes are equal to one:
questions.expl: 1 Terabyte (TB) = 1024 Gigabytes.

questions.text: Which part of the computer is called its 'brain'?
questions.expl: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) processes instructions and performs calculations, so it is often called the 'brain' of the computer.

questions.text: CPU stands for:
questions.expl: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit, the main component that executes instructions.

questions.text: ALU stands for:
questions.expl: ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) is the part of the CPU that performs arithmetic and logical operations.

questions.text: CU stands for:
questions.expl: CU (Control Unit) directs the operation of the processor by controlling the flow of data between the CPU and other components.

questions.text: Which generation of computers used vacuum tubes?
questions.expl: First-generation computers (1940s-50s) used bulky vacuum tubes for circuitry.

questions.text: Which generation of computers used transistors?
questions.expl: Second-generation computers (late 1950s-60s) replaced vacuum tubes with smaller, more reliable transistors.

questions.text: Which generation of computers used Integrated Circuits (ICs)?
questions.expl: Third-generation computers (1960s-70s) used Integrated Circuits (ICs), which packed many transistors onto a single chip.

questions.text: Which generation of computers introduced the microprocessor?
questions.expl: Fourth-generation computers (1970s onward) introduced the microprocessor, putting an entire CPU on one chip.

questions.text: The fifth generation of computers is mainly based on:
questions.expl: Fifth-generation computers focus on Artificial Intelligence, natural language processing, and parallel processing.

questions.text: RAM is an example of:
questions.expl: RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile, meaning its contents are lost when power is switched off.

questions.text: ROM is an example of:
questions.expl: ROM (Read Only Memory) is non-volatile, so it retains data even without power.

questions.text: Which of the following is a secondary storage device?
questions.expl: A hard disk stores data permanently and is a secondary (external to CPU) storage device, unlike RAM.

questions.text: Which memory is used to speed up processor access to data?
questions.expl: Cache memory sits between the CPU and RAM and is much faster, so it speeds up the processor's access to frequently used data.

questions.text: Which of the following is a pure input device?
questions.expl: A keyboard only sends data into the computer, making it a pure input device.

questions.text: Which of the following is a pure output device?
questions.expl: A monitor only displays data from the computer, making it a pure output device.

questions.text: Which device works as both input and output device?
questions.expl: A modem both sends data out (input to the network) and receives data (output to the computer), so it works as both input and output.

questions.text: Which device is used to point and select items on screen?
questions.expl: A mouse is used to point at and select items on the screen, making it a pointing input device.

questions.text: Which device converts digital signals to analog signals and vice versa?
questions.expl: A modem (modulator-demodulator) converts digital signals from a computer into analog signals for transmission, and back again.

questions.text: CD stands for:
questions.expl: CD stands for Compact Disc, an optical storage medium.

questions.text: DVD stands for:
questions.expl: DVD stands for Digital Versatile Disc, which can store more data than a CD.

questions.text: CD and DVD are examples of which type of storage device?
questions.expl: CDs and DVDs use a laser to read/write data, making them optical storage devices.

questions.text: One nibble is equal to:
questions.expl: A nibble equals 4 bits, which is half of a byte (8 bits).

questions.text: The base of the binary number system is:
questions.expl: The binary number system uses only two digits (0 and 1), so its base is 2.

questions.text: The base of the decimal number system is:
questions.expl: The decimal number system uses ten digits (0-9), so its base is 10.

questions.text: The base of the hexadecimal number system is:
questions.expl: The hexadecimal number system uses sixteen symbols (0-9 and A-F), so its base is 16.

questions.text: The base of the octal number system is:
questions.expl: The octal number system uses eight digits (0-7), so its base is 8.

questions.text: The binary equivalent of decimal number 10 is:
questions.expl: Decimal 10 in binary is 1010 (8+0+2+0).

questions.text: Which software manages and controls computer hardware and software resources?
questions.expl: The Operating System manages and controls all hardware and software resources of a computer.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of an operating system?
questions.expl: Windows is a well-known example of an operating system that manages computer resources.

questions.text: MS Word is an example of:
questions.expl: MS Word is application software used for a specific task (word processing), unlike system software such as an OS.

questions.text: Firmware is generally stored in:
questions.expl: Firmware is low-level software stored permanently in ROM chips to control basic hardware functions.

questions.text: BIOS stands for:
questions.expl: BIOS stands for Basic Input Output System, firmware that initializes hardware during booting.

questions.text: POST stands for:
questions.expl: POST stands for Power On Self Test, a diagnostic check the computer runs when it starts up.

questions.text: The process of loading the operating system into memory when a computer starts is called:
questions.expl: Booting is the process of loading the operating system into memory when a computer is switched on.

questions.text: Restarting a computer that is already switched on is called:
questions.expl: A warm boot is restarting a computer that is already on (e.g., via a restart command), without cutting power.

questions.text: Which component connects and allows communication between all parts of a computer?
questions.expl: The motherboard is the main circuit board that connects and allows communication between all internal components.

questions.text: Which port is commonly used nowadays to connect a printer to a computer?
questions.expl: USB ports are the standard modern interface used to connect printers and most other peripherals.

questions.text: USB stands for:
questions.expl: USB stands for Universal Serial Bus, a common standard for connecting peripheral devices.

questions.text: Which device is used to convert a physical document into a digital image?
questions.expl: A scanner captures a physical document and converts it into a digital image.

questions.text: OCR stands for:
questions.expl: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) is technology that converts scanned images of text into editable, machine-readable text.

questions.text: Which of the following is a volatile memory?
questions.expl: RAM loses its data when the power is turned off, which is the defining feature of volatile memory.

questions.text: The BIOS of a computer is usually stored in:
questions.expl: BIOS firmware is stored in ROM so it is available even before the operating system loads.

questions.text: One byte consists of how many bits?
questions.expl: 1 byte is made up of 8 bits.

questions.text: Which of the following is antivirus software?
questions.expl: Quick Heal is a well-known antivirus software brand, unlike the other options which are general-purpose applications.

questions.text: A malicious program that replicates itself and spreads to other files is called a:
questions.expl: A virus is malicious code that attaches itself to files/programs and spreads by replicating when the host file is run.

questions.text: A self-replicating malicious program that does not need a host file is called a:
questions.expl: A worm is self-replicating malware that spreads across networks on its own, without needing to attach to a host file.

questions.text: A malicious program disguised as legitimate software is called a:
questions.expl: A Trojan Horse disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it.

questions.text: Software that automatically displays unwanted advertisements is called:
questions.expl: Adware automatically displays unwanted advertisements on a user's device.

questions.text: Software that secretly monitors and collects user activity is called:
questions.expl: Spyware secretly monitors user activity and collects information without the user's consent.

questions.text: The default file extension of a Microsoft Word document (2007 onwards) is:
questions.expl: Since Word 2007, the default file format for Word documents is .docx.

questions.text: The default file extension of a Microsoft Excel workbook (2007 onwards) is:
questions.expl: Since Excel 2007, the default file format for Excel workbooks is .xlsx.

questions.text: The default file extension of a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation (2007 onwards) is:
questions.expl: Since PowerPoint 2007, the default file format for presentations is .pptx.

questions.text: Which of the following is a common image file extension?
questions.expl: .jpg (JPEG) is a widely used file extension for compressed digital images.

questions.text: Which of the following is a common document file extension used for sharing formatted files?
questions.expl: .pdf (Portable Document Format) is commonly used to share documents while preserving formatting across devices.

questions.text: Which of the following file extensions represents an executable file in Windows?
questions.expl: .exe denotes an executable program file in Windows.

questions.text: Which key is used to delete the character to the left of the cursor?
questions.expl: Backspace deletes the character immediately to the left of the cursor.

questions.text: Which key is used to delete the character to the right of the cursor?
questions.expl: Delete removes the character immediately to the right of the cursor.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+C is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+C copies the selected content to the clipboard.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+V is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+V pastes content from the clipboard at the cursor's position.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+X is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+X cuts the selected content, removing it and copying it to the clipboard.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+Z is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+Z reverses (undoes) the last action performed.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+Y is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+Y redoes an action that was undone.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+S is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+S saves the current file.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+P is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+P opens the print dialog box.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+A is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+A selects all content in the current document or window.

questions.text: In Windows, the F2 key is generally used to:
options: Rename a selected file or folder
questions.expl: F2 is commonly used in Windows Explorer to rename a selected file or folder.

questions.text: In Windows, the F5 key is generally used to:
questions.expl: F5 refreshes the current window or webpage in most Windows applications.

questions.text: Alt+Tab is used to:
questions.expl: Alt+Tab lets users quickly switch between currently open windows/applications.

questions.text: Alt+F4 is used to:
questions.expl: Alt+F4 closes the currently active window or application.

questions.text: Windows key + D is used to:
questions.expl: Windows key + D minimizes all windows and shows the desktop.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an operating system?
questions.expl: MS Word is application software for word processing, not an operating system.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a multitasking operating system?
questions.expl: Windows allows multiple programs to run at once, making it a multitasking operating system.

questions.text: Real-time operating systems are commonly used in:
questions.expl: Real-time operating systems respond within strict time constraints and are widely used in embedded systems like industrial controllers.

questions.text: Windows operating system is developed by:
questions.expl: Windows is developed and maintained by Microsoft.

questions.text: The Linux kernel was originally developed by:
questions.expl: Linus Torvalds originally created the Linux kernel in 1991.

questions.text: Which of the following is an open source operating system?
questions.expl: Linux is open source, meaning its source code is freely available for anyone to view and modify.

questions.text: GUI stands for:
questions.expl: GUI stands for Graphical User Interface, which uses icons, windows, and menus for interaction.

questions.text: CLI stands for:
questions.expl: CLI stands for Command Line Interface, where users type text commands to interact with the system.

questions.text: A compiler is a program that:
options: Translates high-level language code into machine code all at once
questions.expl: A compiler translates the entire high-level source code into machine code in one go before execution.

questions.text: Unlike a compiler, an interpreter:
options: Translates and executes code line by line
Translates the whole program at once
questions.expl: An interpreter translates and executes program code line by line, rather than compiling it all at once.

questions.text: Which of the following is a high-level programming language?
questions.expl: Python is a high-level programming language that is closer to human-readable syntax.

questions.text: Assembly language is an example of a:
questions.expl: Assembly language uses mnemonic instructions close to machine code, making it a low-level language.

questions.text: Machine language instructions are written in:
questions.expl: Machine language is written directly in binary code (0s and 1s) that the CPU can execute directly.

questions.text: Assembly language is often referred to as a:
questions.expl: Assembly language is classified as a Second Generation Language (2GL).

questions.text: In a flowchart, which symbol represents a decision point?
questions.expl: In flowcharts, a diamond shape represents a decision point with branching outcomes (e.g., yes/no).

questions.text: In a flowchart, which symbol represents a process step?
questions.expl: In flowcharts, a rectangle represents a processing step or action.

questions.text: An algorithm is best described as:
options: A step-by-step procedure to solve a problem
questions.expl: An algorithm is a well-defined, step-by-step procedure or set of rules to solve a problem.

questions.text: Which storage device generally provides faster data access, SSD or HDD?
questions.expl: SSDs (Solid State Drives) have no moving parts and generally provide faster data access than mechanical HDDs.

questions.text: SSD stands for:
questions.expl: SSD stands for Solid State Drive, a storage device using flash memory instead of spinning disks.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes a Kilobyte?
questions.expl: A Kilobyte is commonly understood as approximately 1024 bytes in computing (binary convention).

questions.text: A device driver is software that:
options: Allows the operating system to communicate with hardware devices
questions.expl: A device driver is software that enables the operating system to communicate with and control hardware devices.

questions.text: Which of these best describes 'freeware'?
options: Software available with source code editable by anyone
questions.expl: Freeware refers to software that is made available to users free of cost, though its source code is usually not open for modification.

questions.text: Which of the following units is used to measure processor speed?
questions.expl: Processor (CPU) speed is measured in Gigahertz (GHz), indicating clock cycles per second.

questions.text: A set of instructions that tells a computer how to perform a task is called a:
questions.expl: A program is a set of instructions written to direct a computer to perform a specific task.

questions.text: LAN stands for:
questions.expl: LAN stands for Local Area Network, a network confined to a small area like an office or building.

questions.text: WAN stands for:
questions.expl: WAN stands for Wide Area Network, spanning large geographic areas, such as connecting cities or countries.

questions.text: MAN stands for:
questions.expl: MAN stands for Metropolitan Area Network, covering a city or large campus, larger than a LAN but smaller than a WAN.

questions.text: PAN stands for:
questions.expl: PAN stands for Personal Area Network, a very short-range network for personal devices (e.g., Bluetooth devices).

questions.text: The Internet is best described as a network of:
questions.expl: The Internet is a global network made up of many interconnected smaller computer networks.

questions.text: WWW stands for:
questions.expl: WWW stands for World Wide Web, the system of interlinked hypertext documents accessed via the Internet.

questions.text: The World Wide Web was invented by:
questions.expl: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN.

questions.text: HTTP stands for:
questions.expl: HTTP stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol, used to transfer web pages over the Internet.

questions.text: HTTPS differs from HTTP mainly because it provides:
questions.expl: HTTPS adds SSL/TLS encryption to HTTP, providing a secure, encrypted connection between browser and server.

questions.text: FTP stands for:
questions.expl: FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol, used to transfer files between computers over a network.

questions.text: SMTP stands for:
questions.expl: SMTP stands for Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, used to send outgoing email messages.

questions.text: TCP/IP stands for:
questions.expl: TCP/IP stands for Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol, the fundamental suite of protocols governing internet communication.

questions.text: Which IP address version is most commonly used today?
questions.expl: IPv4 remains the most widely used IP addressing version, though IPv6 adoption is growing.

questions.text: An IPv4 address consists of how many bits?
questions.expl: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, typically written as four decimal numbers (e.g., 192.168.1.1).

questions.text: An IPv6 address consists of how many bits?
questions.expl: An IPv6 address is 128 bits long, designed to provide a much larger address space than IPv4.

questions.text: Which device is used to connect different networks together and direct data traffic?
questions.expl: A router connects different networks and directs data packets between them to reach their destination.

questions.text: Which device broadcasts incoming data to all connected devices in a network?
questions.expl: A hub broadcasts incoming data to all connected devices on a network, regardless of the intended recipient.

questions.text: Which device sends data only to the specific device it is intended for?
questions.expl: A switch intelligently forwards data only to the specific device it is addressed to, unlike a hub.

questions.text: Which device converts digital signals to analog for transmission over telephone lines?
questions.expl: A modem converts digital computer signals into analog signals (and vice versa) for transmission over telephone lines.

questions.text: Which device is used to boost or regenerate a weak network signal?
questions.expl: A repeater regenerates and boosts a weak or degraded network signal so it can travel further.

questions.text: In which network topology are all devices connected to a central hub or switch?
questions.expl: In a star topology, every device connects individually to a central hub or switch.

questions.text: In which network topology are devices connected in a circular chain?
questions.expl: In a ring topology, each device connects to exactly two others, forming a circular data path.

questions.text: In which network topology do all devices share a single common cable (backbone)?
questions.expl: In a bus topology, all devices share a single common communication cable (the backbone).

questions.text: In which network topology is every device connected to every other device?
questions.expl: In a mesh topology, every device is directly connected to every other device, providing high redundancy.

questions.text: The OSI model consists of how many layers?
questions.expl: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model has 7 layers, from Physical up to Application.

questions.text: Which is the first (lowest) layer of the OSI model?
questions.expl: The Physical layer is the lowest (first) layer of the OSI model, dealing with raw bit transmission over hardware.

questions.text: Which is the topmost layer of the OSI model?
questions.expl: The Application layer is the topmost (7th) layer of the OSI model, closest to the end user.

questions.text: The TCP/IP model consists of how many layers?
questions.expl: The TCP/IP model is simplified into 4 layers: Network Access, Internet, Transport, and Application.

questions.text: DNS stands for:
questions.expl: DNS stands for Domain Name System, the internet's directory service for domain names.

questions.text: The main function of DNS is to:
options: Convert domain names into IP addresses
questions.expl: DNS translates human-friendly domain names (like google.com) into numeric IP addresses that computers use.

questions.text: URL stands for:
questions.expl: URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator, the address used to locate a resource on the web.

questions.text: The default port number for HTTP is:
questions.expl: HTTP uses port 80 by default for unencrypted web traffic.

questions.text: The default port number for HTTPS is:
questions.expl: HTTPS uses port 443 by default for secure, encrypted web traffic.

questions.text: The default port number for FTP is:
questions.expl: FTP uses port 21 by default for file transfer control.

questions.text: The default port number for SMTP is:
questions.expl: SMTP uses port 25 by default for sending email.

questions.text: Which protocol is commonly used to download/receive email from a mail server?
questions.expl: POP3 is a protocol commonly used to download email from a mail server to a local device.

questions.text: POP3 stands for:
questions.expl: POP3 stands for Post Office Protocol version 3, used for retrieving email.

questions.text: IMAP stands for:
questions.expl: IMAP stands for Internet Message Access Protocol, which lets users access and manage email directly on the server.

questions.text: Which of the following is a web browser?
questions.expl: Google Chrome is a web browser used to access and view websites.

questions.text: Which of the following is a popular search engine?
questions.expl: Google is one of the most widely used search engines for finding information online.

questions.text: Google Chrome is developed by:
questions.expl: Google Chrome is developed and maintained by Google.

questions.text: Small text files stored by a web browser to remember user information are called:
questions.expl: Cookies are small text files that websites store in a browser to remember user preferences and information.

questions.text: Temporary storage of web page data on a browser to speed up future visits is called:
questions.expl: Browser cache temporarily stores web page data locally so pages load faster on repeat visits.

questions.text: A firewall is primarily used to protect a network from:
questions.expl: A firewall monitors and controls incoming/outgoing network traffic to block unauthorized access.

questions.text: VPN stands for:
questions.expl: VPN stands for Virtual Private Network, which extends a private network across a public network.

questions.text: A VPN is mainly used to:
options: Create a secure private connection over a public network
questions.expl: A VPN creates a secure, encrypted connection ('tunnel') over a public network like the internet.

questions.text: Wi-Fi is generally understood to stand for:
questions.expl: Wi-Fi is commonly understood as standing for Wireless Fidelity, a wireless networking technology.

questions.text: The typical range of Bluetooth connectivity is approximately:
questions.expl: Bluetooth typically has a short range of around 10 metres, suited for connecting nearby personal devices.

questions.text: Wi-Fi networks commonly operate on which frequency bands?
questions.expl: Wi-Fi networks commonly operate on the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequency bands.

questions.text: The IEEE standard for wireless LAN (Wi-Fi) is:
questions.expl: IEEE 802.11 is the family of standards that defines Wi-Fi wireless LAN technology.

questions.text: The cable commonly used for wired LAN connections is called:
questions.expl: Ethernet cable is the standard cable type used for wired LAN connections.

questions.text: The RJ45 connector is commonly used for:
questions.expl: RJ45 is the standard connector used to terminate Ethernet/LAN cables.

questions.text: In which topology does the failure of the central device bring down the entire network?
questions.expl: In a star topology, if the central hub/switch fails, the entire network goes down since all devices depend on it.

questions.text: Network bandwidth is generally measured in:
questions.expl: Network bandwidth (data capacity) is measured in bits per second (bps).

questions.text: Internet data transfer speed is commonly expressed in:
questions.expl: Internet speeds are commonly expressed in Mbps (Megabits per second).

questions.text: A search engine primarily helps users to:
questions.expl: A search engine helps users find information and websites on the internet based on search queries.

questions.text: Search engines use automated programs to scan and index web pages, called:
questions.expl: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers or bots to scan and index web pages.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of an e-commerce website?
questions.expl: Amazon is a well-known e-commerce website where goods are bought and sold online.

questions.text: Which protocol is commonly used for secure, encrypted data transfer on websites?
questions.expl: HTTPS uses encryption to provide secure data transfer between a browser and a website.

questions.text: SSL stands for:
questions.expl: SSL stands for Secure Sockets Layer, a protocol for encrypting data sent over a network.

questions.text: Gaining unauthorized access to a computer system or network is known as:
questions.expl: Hacking refers to gaining unauthorized access to a computer system or network.

questions.text: A fraudulent attempt to obtain sensitive information by pretending to be a trustworthy source is called:
questions.expl: Phishing is a fraudulent technique where attackers pose as trustworthy entities to steal sensitive information.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a networking device?
questions.expl: A keyboard is an input device, not a networking device like a router, switch, or hub.

questions.text: A gateway is used to:
questions.expl: A gateway connects networks that use different protocols, translating data between them.

questions.text: Which class of IP address is typically used for very large networks?
questions.expl: Class A IP addresses provide the largest number of host addresses and are used for very large networks.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a private IP address range?
questions.expl: 192.168.x.x is a reserved range used for private (internal) IP addresses.

questions.text: The loopback IP address used to test a computer's own network configuration is:
questions.expl: 127.0.0.1 is the standard loopback address used to test a device's own network stack.

questions.text: Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network?
questions.expl: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices as they join a network.

questions.text: DHCP stands for:
questions.expl: DHCP stands for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol.

questions.text: A MAC address is typically how many bits long?
questions.expl: A MAC address is typically 48 bits (6 bytes) long, uniquely identifying a network interface.

questions.text: NIC stands for:
questions.expl: NIC stands for Network Interface Card, the hardware that connects a computer to a network.

questions.text: Which transmission medium uses pulses of light to carry data?
questions.expl: Fiber optic cable transmits data as pulses of light through glass or plastic fibers.

questions.text: Which of the following provides the fastest data transmission over long distances?
questions.expl: Fiber optic cable offers the fastest and most reliable data transmission over long distances among common media.

questions.text: A network model where a dedicated server provides resources to client computers is called:
questions.expl: In a client-server network, dedicated server(s) provide resources and services to multiple client computers.

questions.text: Cloud computing refers to:
options: Storing and accessing data/applications over the internet
Storing data only on a local hard disk
questions.expl: Cloud computing means storing and accessing data and applications over the internet instead of a local hard drive.

questions.text: Which of the following is a popular cloud storage service?
questions.expl: Google Drive is a widely used cloud storage service for storing and sharing files online.

questions.text: Gmail is an email service provided by:
questions.expl: Gmail is Google's free email service.

questions.text: In an email address, the '@' symbol separates the:
questions.expl: The '@' symbol in an email address separates the username from the domain name.

questions.text: Which of the following is a valid email address format?
questions.expl: A valid email address follows the format username@domain.com, such as example@gmail.com.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a social media platform?
questions.expl: Facebook is a well-known social media platform for connecting and sharing with others online.

questions.text: VoIP is technology used to make calls over the internet. VoIP stands for:
questions.expl: VoIP stands for Voice over Internet Protocol, technology that enables voice calls over the internet.

questions.text: Terms like 4G and 5G refer to the:
questions.expl: 4G and 5G refer to successive generations of mobile network technology, each offering improved speed and capacity.

questions.text: A router primarily works at which layer of the OSI model?
questions.expl: Routers operate primarily at the Network layer (Layer 3) of the OSI model, using IP addresses to route data.

questions.text: A switch primarily works at which layer of the OSI model?
questions.expl: Switches operate primarily at the Data Link layer (Layer 2), using MAC addresses to forward data.

questions.text: A hub primarily works at which layer of the OSI model?
questions.expl: Hubs operate at the Physical layer (Layer 1), simply broadcasting electrical signals without addressing.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a web browser other than Chrome?
questions.expl: Mozilla Firefox is a popular web browser, an alternative to Google Chrome.

questions.text: The domain extension '.com' generally represents:
questions.expl: The '.com' domain extension generally denotes commercial organizations.

questions.text: The domain extension '.org' generally represents:
questions.expl: The '.org' domain extension is generally used by organizations, often non-profits.

questions.text: The domain extension '.gov' generally represents:
questions.expl: The '.gov' domain extension is reserved for government bodies.

questions.text: The domain extension '.edu' generally represents:
questions.expl: The '.edu' domain extension is generally used by educational institutions.

questions.text: The domain extension '.in' generally represents websites registered in:
questions.expl: The '.in' domain extension generally indicates a website registered in India.

questions.text: Which protocol is a secure alternative to FTP for transferring files?
questions.expl: SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) is a secure alternative to standard FTP for transferring files.

questions.text: Unsolicited and unwanted email, usually sent in bulk, is called:
questions.expl: Spam refers to unsolicited, often bulk, email messages sent without the recipient's consent.

questions.text: A firewall can exist as:
questions.expl: A firewall can be implemented as hardware, software, or a combination of both.

questions.text: Antivirus software is mainly used to protect a computer from:
questions.expl: Antivirus software is designed to detect, prevent, and remove viruses and other malware.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of antivirus software?
questions.expl: Norton is a well-known brand of antivirus software.

questions.text: Encryption is the process of converting data into:
questions.expl: Encryption converts readable data into a coded, unreadable form to protect it from unauthorized access.

questions.text: Decryption is the process of:
options: Converting encrypted data back into readable form
questions.expl: Decryption is the reverse process of converting encrypted data back into its original, readable form.

questions.text: Which type of network typically covers a single building or campus?
questions.expl: A LAN (Local Area Network) typically covers a single building or campus.

questions.text: An Internet Service Provider (ISP) is a company that:
options: Provides users with access to the internet
questions.expl: An ISP (Internet Service Provider) is a company that provides individuals and organizations access to the internet.

questions.text: The default file extension used by Microsoft Word 2016 is:
questions.expl: Since Word 2007, the default file format is .docx.

questions.text: Microsoft Word is developed by:
questions.expl: Microsoft Word is developed and maintained by Microsoft as part of MS Office.

questions.text: In recent versions of MS Word, the default font is:
questions.expl: Recent versions of MS Word use Calibri as the default font.

questions.text: The Home tab in MS Word mainly contains options for:
questions.expl: The Home tab in Word mainly holds font and paragraph formatting options like bold, alignment, and styles.

questions.text: Tables, pictures, and headers/footers are inserted from which tab in MS Word?
questions.expl: Tables, pictures, headers, and footers are all inserted using commands on the Insert tab.

questions.text: What creates repeating information like a logo or date on every page of a Word document?
questions.expl: A Header/Footer displays repeating content, like a logo or date, automatically on every page.

questions.text: Mail Merge in MS Word is mainly used to:
options: Merge two Word files into one
Send personalised letters to multiple recipients
questions.expl: Mail Merge combines a template letter with a data source to create personalised copies for multiple recipients.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+B in MS Word applies:
questions.expl: Ctrl+B applies or removes bold formatting to selected text.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+I in MS Word applies:
questions.expl: Ctrl+I applies or removes italic formatting to selected text.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+U in MS Word applies:
questions.expl: Ctrl+U applies or removes underline formatting to selected text.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+N in MS Word is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+N opens a new blank document.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+O in MS Word is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+O opens the dialog to open an existing document.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+W in MS Word is used to:
options: Save the document as a Web page
questions.expl: Ctrl+W closes the currently open document.

questions.text: The F7 key in MS Word is generally used to:
questions.expl: F7 launches the Spelling and Grammar check tool in Word.

questions.text: Which view in MS Word shows the document exactly as it will appear when printed?
questions.expl: Print Layout view shows the document exactly as it will look when printed, including margins and page breaks.

questions.text: The Track Changes feature in MS Word is used to:
questions.expl: Track Changes records every edit (insertions, deletions, formatting) made by reviewers for later approval or rejection.

questions.text: Which feature in MS Word automatically highlights spelling and grammar errors while typing?
questions.expl: The built-in Spelling and Grammar check underlines errors automatically as the user types.

questions.text: The Word Count feature in MS Word is generally found under the:
questions.expl: Word Count is generally accessed through the Review tab (also shown in the status bar).

questions.text: Which feature is used to combine multiple selected cells into one cell in a Word table?
questions.expl: Merge Cells combines multiple selected table cells into a single larger cell.

questions.text: The Thesaurus tool in MS Word is used to:
options: Find synonyms of a selected word
questions.expl: The Thesaurus tool suggests synonyms and related words for a selected term.

questions.text: Which are the two common page orientation options in MS Word?
questions.expl: Portrait (tall) and Landscape (wide) are the two standard page orientation options.

questions.text: Page numbers can be inserted in MS Word from the:
questions.expl: Page numbers are inserted via the Insert tab, using the Page Number command in the Header & Footer group.

questions.text: Which feature is used to create a bulleted list in MS Word?
questions.expl: Bullets format a list with symbols rather than numbers, applied from the Home tab.

questions.text: The Watermark feature in MS Word is generally found under the:
questions.expl: Watermark is found under the Design tab and adds faint background text or images to pages.

questions.text: Which shortcut key selects the entire content of a Word document?
questions.expl: Ctrl+A selects all the content within the current document.

questions.text: Which feature is used to change selected text to UPPERCASE, lowercase, or Title Case?
questions.expl: Change Case lets users quickly switch selected text between UPPERCASE, lowercase, and Title Case.

questions.text: A Table of Contents in MS Word is typically generated using:
options: Heading styles and the References tab
questions.expl: A Table of Contents is auto-generated from headings (formatted with Heading styles) using the References tab.

questions.text: Which feature in MS Word allows reviewers to add remarks without editing the original text?
questions.expl: Comments allow reviewers to add notes or remarks alongside text without altering the original content.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+H in MS Word is used to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+H opens the Find and Replace dialog box.

questions.text: The shortcut key Ctrl+F in MS Word opens the:
questions.expl: Ctrl+F opens the Find dialog box to search for text within the document.

questions.text: The Styles gallery in MS Word is generally found on the:
questions.expl: The Styles gallery, offering quick formatting presets like Heading 1 and Normal, is located on the Home tab.

questions.text: Mathematical equations can be inserted in MS Word from the:
questions.expl: Mathematical equations are inserted through the Equation command on the Insert tab.

questions.text: The Ribbon interface in MS Word is organised into:
questions.expl: The Word Ribbon is organised into tabs (e.g., Home, Insert), each containing groups of related commands.

questions.text: Before .docx, the older default Word file format (used until Word 2003) was:
questions.expl: Before .docx, Word used the .doc format as its default (up through Word 2003).

questions.text: The Clipboard in MS Office applications temporarily stores:
questions.expl: The Clipboard temporarily holds content that has been copied or cut, ready to be pasted elsewhere.

questions.text: The default file extension used by Microsoft Excel 2016 is:
questions.expl: Since Excel 2007, the default workbook file format is .xlsx.

questions.text: Microsoft Excel is best described as a type of:
questions.expl: Microsoft Excel is a spreadsheet application used for organizing, calculating, and analyzing data in a grid of cells.

questions.text: The intersection of a row and a column in Excel is called a:
questions.expl: A cell is formed where a row and column intersect, and it holds a single piece of data or formula.

questions.text: The Formula Bar in Excel displays the:
questions.expl: The Formula Bar shows the actual content (value or formula) of the currently selected (active) cell.

questions.text: Every formula in Excel must begin with the symbol:
questions.expl: Every Excel formula must start with an equals sign (=) so Excel recognises it as a calculation.

questions.text: The SUM function in Excel is used to:
questions.expl: The SUM function adds together a specified range of numeric values.

questions.text: The COUNTA function in MS Excel counts:
questions.expl: COUNTA counts all non-empty cells in a range, regardless of whether they contain text or numbers.

questions.text: The COUNT function in MS Excel counts:
questions.expl: COUNT counts only the cells in a range that contain numeric values.

questions.text: The COUNTBLANK function in MS Excel counts:
questions.expl: COUNTBLANK counts the number of empty (blank) cells in a specified range.

questions.text: The AVERAGE function in Excel calculates the:
options: Sum of a range of numbers
Mean of a range of numbers
questions.expl: AVERAGE calculates the arithmetic mean of a range of numeric values.

questions.text: The MAX function in Excel returns the:
questions.expl: MAX returns the largest numeric value within a specified range.

questions.text: The MIN function in Excel returns the:
questions.expl: MIN returns the smallest numeric value within a specified range.

questions.text: The IF function in Excel is an example of a:
questions.expl: IF is a logical function that returns one value if a condition is true and another if it is false.

questions.text: The VLOOKUP function searches for a value in the:
options: First column of a range, vertically
First row of a range, horizontally
questions.expl: VLOOKUP looks up a value in the first (leftmost) column of a range and returns a value from a specified column in the same row (vertical lookup).

questions.text: The HLOOKUP function searches for a value in the:
options: First column of a range, vertically
First row of a range, horizontally
questions.expl: HLOOKUP looks up a value in the first (top) row of a range and returns a value from a specified row in the same column (horizontal lookup).

questions.text: In Excel formulas, the symbol used to create an absolute cell reference is:
questions.expl: The dollar sign ($) is used before the column and/or row reference to make it an absolute (fixed) reference.

questions.text: The reference $A$1 in Excel is an example of a/an:
questions.expl: $A$1 fixes both the column and row, so the reference does not change when the formula is copied - this is an absolute reference.

questions.text: The reference A1 (without dollar signs) in Excel is an example of a/an:
questions.expl: A1 (no dollar signs) is a relative reference, which automatically adjusts when the formula is copied to other cells.

questions.text: Which key is used to toggle between relative and absolute cell references while editing a formula?
questions.expl: Pressing F4 while editing a formula cycles through relative, absolute, and mixed reference styles for the selected cell reference.

questions.text: Charts in Excel are inserted from which tab?
questions.expl: Charts are inserted using commands found on the Insert tab.

questions.text: A pie chart in Excel is best used to show:
options: The proportion of parts to a whole
questions.expl: A pie chart visually represents how individual parts contribute to a whole (as proportions/percentages).

questions.text: Which shortcut key is used to insert a new worksheet in Excel?
questions.expl: Shift+F11 inserts a new worksheet in the current workbook.

questions.text: Pressing Ctrl+Home in Excel moves the cursor to:
questions.expl: Ctrl+Home moves the cursor directly to cell A1 of the active worksheet.

questions.text: Which function is used to join text from multiple cells into one in Excel?
questions.expl: CONCATENATE (or the newer CONCAT/TEXTJOIN) joins text from multiple cells into a single cell.

questions.text: Sorting data in Excel arranges it in:
questions.expl: Sorting rearranges data rows in ascending or descending order based on selected column(s).

questions.text: The Filter feature in Excel is used to:
options: Display only data meeting specific criteria
questions.expl: The Filter feature temporarily hides rows that do not meet specified criteria, showing only matching data.

questions.text: Conditional Formatting in Excel is used to:
options: Protect a worksheet with a password
Format cells automatically based on specified conditions
questions.expl: Conditional Formatting automatically applies formatting (like colour) to cells that meet specified conditions.

questions.text: The Freeze Panes feature in Excel is used to:
options: Keep specific rows/columns visible while scrolling
Lock the entire workbook with a password
questions.expl: Freeze Panes keeps selected rows and/or columns visible on screen while the rest of the worksheet scrolls.

questions.text: The file extension used for a macro-enabled Excel workbook is:
questions.expl: Macro-enabled Excel workbooks are saved with the .xlsm extension, which supports embedded VBA macros.

questions.text: Which shortcut key selects an entire row in Excel?
questions.expl: Shift+Space selects the entire row containing the active cell.

questions.text: Which shortcut key selects an entire column in Excel?
questions.expl: Ctrl+Space selects the entire column containing the active cell.

questions.text: The Name Box in Excel displays the:
options: Reference or name of the currently selected cell
Name of the currently open workbook
questions.expl: The Name Box, located to the left of the Formula Bar, shows the reference or defined name of the selected cell.

questions.text: Which Excel function is used to count the number of characters in a cell?
questions.expl: The LEN function returns the number of characters in a text string within a cell.

questions.text: Which Excel function is used to round a number to a specified number of digits?
questions.expl: The ROUND function rounds a number to a specified number of decimal places.

questions.text: A new Excel workbook (modern default) generally opens with how many worksheets?
questions.expl: By default, a new Excel workbook now opens with a single worksheet (Sheet1).

questions.text: The default file extension used by Microsoft PowerPoint 2016 is:
questions.expl: Since PowerPoint 2007, the default file format for presentations is .pptx.

questions.text: Microsoft PowerPoint is mainly used to create:
questions.expl: Microsoft PowerPoint is used to create slide-based presentations for sharing information visually.

questions.text: Special effects used to introduce slides in a presentation are called:
questions.expl: Transitions are the special effects that play when moving from one slide to the next.

questions.text: Effects applied to individual text or objects on a slide are called:
questions.expl: Animations are effects applied to individual text or objects within a single slide.

questions.text: Which view in PowerPoint displays all slides as small thumbnails for easy rearranging?
questions.expl: Slide Sorter view displays all slides as small thumbnails, making it easy to rearrange or delete slides.

questions.text: Which view in PowerPoint is generally used to edit the content of an individual slide?
questions.expl: Normal view is the main editing view used to work on the content of one slide at a time.

questions.text: Which view displays the presentation as a full-screen show for the audience?
questions.expl: Slide Show view runs the presentation full-screen, as the audience would see it.

questions.text: Pressing the F5 key in PowerPoint:
options: Starts the slide show from the beginning
Starts the slide show from the current slide
questions.expl: Pressing F5 starts the slide show from the very first slide.

questions.text: Pressing Shift+F5 in PowerPoint:
options: Starts the slide show from the beginning
Starts the slide show from the current slide
questions.expl: Pressing Shift+F5 starts the slide show from the currently selected slide, not the beginning.

questions.text: The Slide Master in PowerPoint is used to:
options: Apply consistent formatting and layout to all slides
questions.expl: The Slide Master controls the layout, fonts, and formatting applied consistently across all slides.

questions.text: Slide transition options in PowerPoint are found under the:
questions.expl: Transition effects and their settings are found on the Transitions tab.

questions.text: Animation options in PowerPoint are found under the:
questions.expl: Animation effects and their settings are found on the Animations tab.

questions.text: The shortcut key to insert a new slide in PowerPoint is:
questions.expl: Ctrl+M inserts a new slide into the presentation.

questions.text: Notes that a presenter can see but the audience cannot are called:
questions.expl: Speaker Notes are notes visible only to the presenter (in Presenter View), not to the audience.

questions.text: To insert a new text box in PowerPoint, you generally use:
questions.expl: A new text box is added via Insert tab > Text Box, then drawn onto the slide.

questions.text: Printed copies of slides given to the audience are called:
questions.expl: Handouts are printed versions of the slides, often with space for notes, given to the audience.

questions.text: The file extension used for a PowerPoint Show that opens directly in slide show mode is:
questions.expl: The .ppsx extension saves a presentation as a PowerPoint Show, which opens directly in slide show mode.

questions.text: The pane that displays thumbnails of all slides on the left side in Normal view is called the:
questions.expl: The Slides pane on the left in Normal view shows thumbnail previews of all slides for quick navigation.

questions.text: Which feature in PowerPoint is used to record narration along with slide timings?
questions.expl: Record Slide Show captures narration, timing, and (optionally) video as the presenter goes through the slides.

questions.text: The Design tab in PowerPoint is mainly used to:
options: Apply themes and templates to the presentation
questions.expl: The Design tab is used to apply overall themes, colour schemes, and templates to the presentation.

questions.text: Which key is generally used to end a running slide show in PowerPoint?
questions.expl: Pressing Esc during a slide show ends the presentation and returns to the editing view.

questions.text: SmartArt in PowerPoint is used to:
options: Create visual diagrams and graphics from text
questions.expl: SmartArt converts bullet-point text into visual diagrams like flowcharts, cycles, and hierarchies.

questions.text: Which feature allows a slide to be skipped during a presentation without deleting it?
questions.expl: Hide Slide marks a slide to be skipped during the presentation without deleting it from the file.

questions.text: The setting used to control automatic slide advancement after a fixed time is found in the:
options: Themes group under the Design tab
Font group under the Home tab
Illustrations group under the Insert tab
Timing group under the Transitions tab
questions.expl: Automatic slide advance timing is set in the Timing group under the Transitions tab.

questions.text: Custom Animation in PowerPoint allows the user to:
options: Apply and customise animation effects on objects
Change the slide background colour only
questions.expl: Custom Animation lets users apply and fine-tune animation effects (entrance, emphasis, exit) on slide objects.

questions.text: Audio can be added to a PowerPoint slide from the:
questions.expl: Audio clips are inserted into a slide via the Insert tab.

questions.text: Video can be added to a PowerPoint slide from the:
questions.expl: Video clips are inserted into a slide via the Insert tab.

questions.text: Which shortcut key duplicates the currently selected slide in PowerPoint?
questions.expl: Ctrl+D duplicates the currently selected slide.

questions.text: Ready-made colour and formatting combinations applied to a presentation are called:
questions.expl: Themes are pre-designed combinations of colours, fonts, and effects applied to give a presentation a consistent look.

questions.text: The default aspect ratio of slides in modern versions of PowerPoint is:
questions.expl: Modern PowerPoint presentations default to a 16:9 widescreen aspect ratio.
